title: History 3: Pixel by pixel, autoregressive image models

questions.q: In the context of autoregressive image models, what is the primary trade-off compared to diffusion models?
options: Autoregressive models sacrifice speed for rigorous, token-by-token construction of reality.
Autoregressive models sacrifice precision for parallel processing speed.
Autoregressive models sacrifice global consistency for local detail.
Autoregressive models sacrifice memory usage for faster inference.
questions.answer: Autoregressive models sacrifice speed for rigorous, token-by-token construction of reality.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'Autoregressive models sacrifice speed for a rigorous, token-by-token construction of reality.' It contrasts this with diffusion models which 'sacrifice sequential context for speed.'

questions.q: How does the causal mask function in an autoregressive image model when predicting pixel i?
options: It allows the model to attend to pixels 0 through i-1, while remaining blind to pixels i+1 through N.
It allows the model to attend to all pixels in the image simultaneously to ensure global consistency.
It restricts the model to only attending to the immediate previous pixel i-1.
It allows the model to attend to future pixels i+1 through N to predict the current pixel.
questions.answer: It allows the model to attend to pixels 0 through i-1, while remaining blind to pixels i+1 through N.
questions.why: The lesson explains: 'When the model predicts pixel i, it is allowed to "attend" to pixels 0 through i-1. It is blind to pixels i+1 through N.'

questions.q: In the provided lab simulation, why is the prediction for the first pixel (pred_0) equal to 0?
options: Because the first pixel in the image is always zero by definition.
Because the model defaults to 0 when there is no previous history (cold start).
Because the mean of an empty set is defined as 0 in PyTorch.
Because the causal mask blocks all inputs for the first step.
questions.answer: Because the model defaults to 0 when there is no previous history (cold start).
questions.why: The lab analysis states: 'RESULT pred_0 = 0: The first pixel has no history. The model defaults to 0. This proves the cold start problem of autoregression: the first token is generated without context.'

questions.q: What is the specific role of the PixelTokenEmbedder module in the PixDiT architecture described in the lesson?
options: It processes 16x16 latent patches to reduce computational load.
It lifts each individual RGB pixel to the hidden size, allowing for fine-grained sequential or local attention.
It injects low-quality latent features into the pixel-level transformer.
It applies rotary positional encoding to the entire image grid.
questions.answer: It lifts each individual RGB pixel to the hidden size, allowing for fine-grained sequential or local attention.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'PixelTokenEmbedder: This module lifts each individual RGB pixel to the hidden size... Instead of processing a 16x16 latent patch, it processes individual pixels, allowing for fine-grained sequential or local attention.'

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is a common mistake regarding the definition of 'autoregressive' in modern image models?
options: Assuming that autoregressive models always process individual pixels rather than patches or tokens.
Believing that diffusion models are strictly sequential in their inference process.
Thinking that causal masking is unnecessary for autoregressive models.
Assuming that PixelRNN and PixelCNN are the most common models in standard ComfyUI workflows.
questions.answer: Assuming that autoregressive models always process individual pixels rather than patches or tokens.
questions.why: The 'Common mistakes' section states: 'Many students assume "autoregressive" means "slow." While true for pixel-level autoregression... modern models often autoregress over patches or tokens, not individual pixels.'
